extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Montaigne / readers of personal, philosophical essays
extracted.subtask_description: A personal, philosophical essay reflecting on conduct, conversation, friendship, aging, and the uses of books and solitude; modeled on Montaigne's style of self-observation and moral reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel's force depends on timing
rubrics_metrics.description: "The force of all counsel consists in the time; occasions and things eternally shift and change."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate advice by whether it fitted the circumstances when given; outcomes that change later do not necessarily invalidate the counsel. Montaigne uses Phocion's example: if an advised course fails later, that is not cause to repent of having advised it. Anti-pattern: judging past counsel solely by later events without considering contemporaneous facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give advice candidly and clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: "When any of my friends address themselves to me for advice, I give it candidly and clearly, without sticking..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide honest, unreserved counsel even if the outcome may reproach you; accept the risk of being blamed rather than withholding help. Example: speak plainly rather than hedging to avoid future reproach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit others only for special expertise or facts
rubrics_metrics.description: "I seldom solicit the advice of another, if not by honour of ceremony, or excepting where I stand in need of information, special science, or as to matter of fact."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely primarily on your own judgment for matters of taste or general judgment; consult others when you lack specific knowledge or factual information. Anti-pattern: importing others' opinions as substitutes for your own judgment in matters you can judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept limits of prudence and avoid self-blame for unforeseeable events
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are secret, and not to be foreseen, parts in matters we have in hand... if my prudence could not penetrate into nor foresee them, I blame it not: 'tis commissioned no further than its own limits."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate bad outcomes with moral failure when hidden contingencies existed. Distinguish between errors of judgment and unavoidable misfortune; blame fortune, not necessarily your counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not indulge in incidental repentance of old age
rubrics_metrics.description: "I abominate that incidental repentance which old age brings along with it... I can never think myself beholden to impotency for any good it can do to me."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist treating bodily decline as moral improvement. Anti-pattern: claiming virtue simply because appetites have waned due to infirmity; value moral reform that springs from reason, not debility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance and chastity should be valued for their own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: "We ought to love temperance for itself, and because God has commanded that and chastity; but that which we are reduced to by catarrhs... is neither chastity nor temperance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess motives: virtue motivated by conviction is genuine; virtue imposed by physical incapacity is not. Example: avoid counting inability to indulge as moral merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume greater wisdom merely from age
rubrics_metrics.description: "I find my reason the very same it was in my most licentious age... I do not discern that in itself it judges anything otherwise now than it formerly did"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate someone's present judgments by their quality, not by their age. Anti-pattern: automatically deference to elderly opinion because of age alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against the vices of senility (pride, superstition, envy)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Besides a foolish and feeble pride, an impertinent prating, froward and insociable humours, superstition, and a ridiculous desire of riches... I find there more envy, injustice, and malice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and resist mental and moral deteriorations that can accompany aging; require study and precaution to weaken their progress. Practical guidance: active study and self-examination to counteract these tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have variety and pliancy of mind; avoid being riveted to one temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our chiefest sufficiency is to know how to apply ourselves to divers employments... 'Tis to be, but not to live, to keep a man's self tied and bound by necessity to one only course; those are the bravest souls that have in them the most variety and pliancy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value intellectual and practical flexibility; cultivate multiple interests and capacities. Anti-pattern: fixing yourself rigidly to one role or self-image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ mind to various matters rather than clinging to idleness
rubrics_metrics.description: "Idleness is to me a very painful labour... Most men's minds require foreign matter to exercise and enliven them; mine has rather need of it to sit still and repose itself... Meditation is a powerful and full study."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage varied intellectual employment: meditation, reading, conversation, and action. Consider meditation as serious work of the mind. Anti-pattern: trivial chatter or passive idleness that untrains the faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reading to rouse reason and employ judgment, not just memory
rubrics_metrics.description: "The principal use of reading to me is, that by various objects it rouses my reason, and employs my judgment, not my memory."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer reading that stimulates thinking and judgement over mere accumulation of facts. Evaluate books by their capacity to provoke analysis and reflection. Practical note: avoid rote learning; read widely to enliven thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt conversation to your audience; avoid pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: "You must let yourself down to those with whom you converse... The learned often stumble at this stone; they will always be parading their pedantic science..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In social discourse, favor natural, simple expression suited to listeners rather than ostentatious display of learning. Anti-pattern: quoting authorities or using learned terms to show off in trivial company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate desires to what is nearest and attainable
rubrics_metrics.description: "We must moderate and adapt our desires to the nearest and easiest to be acquired things."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate projects and ambitions by plausibility and proximity. Anti-pattern: separating oneself from many because of fantastical or impractical attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be able to converse pleasantly with people of all ranks, including servants
rubrics_metrics.description: "I envy those who can render themselves familiar with the meanest of their followers, and talk with them in their own way... It is inhuman and unjust to set so great a value upon this pitiful prerogative of fortune."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social skill includes ease with people of different stations; adopt humility and occasional familiarity rather than perpetual magisterial tone. Practical tip: sometimes affect ignorance or be facetious to bridge divides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nobility should use their natural graces rather than borrowed arts
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is a great folly to put out their own light and shine by a borrowed lustre... they conceal and cover their beauties under others that are none of theirs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage authenticity: use what is genuinely yours (manners, presence) rather than attempting to mask with technical arts (rhetoric, law) unsuitable to your role. Anti-pattern: nobles parading technical learning to be governed by those who teach them.

rubrics_metrics.name: In love, bodily beauty and grace often outweigh wit
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the subject of love, a subject principally relating to the senses of seeing and touching, something may be done without the graces of the mind: without the graces of the body, nothing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating attraction, acknowledge the primacy of physical appeal; do not overvalue intellect alone in matters of sensual love. Caveat: Montaigne notes this is about human tendency, not moral prescription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books are a constant and reliable comfort—keep them at hand
rubrics_metrics.description: "The third, is much more certain, and much more our own... 'Tis the best viaticum I have yet found out for this human journey... I never travel without books..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value books as durable companions that provide solace, diversion, and intellectual sustenance. Practical guidance: maintain a personal library and access to reading during travel and solitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange a private space at home for solitude and study
rubrics_metrics.description: "That man, in my opinion, is very miserable, who has not at home where to be by himself... 'Tis in the third storey of a tower... There I pass away both most of the days of my life..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create and maintain a physical retreat (study/library) from which you can observe household life while preserving solitude. Guidance includes layout (view of garden, plenty of light, walking gallery) and behavioral norms (no ceremonial restrictions among guests there).

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship and good conversation aim at privacy, conference, and exercise of souls
rubrics_metrics.description: "The end of this commerce is simply privacy, frequentation and conference, the exercise of souls, without other fruit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value friendships that allow mature, free, good-humoured exchange across subjects; judge a friendship by the quality of shared judgment, gaiety, and freedom rather than by utility or status. Example: better to discover a friend's mind at table than in council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humble learning when among friends—be suffragan and docile
rubrics_metrics.description: "If learning please to step into our talk, it shall not be rejected, not magisterial, imperious, and importunate, as-it commonly is, but suffragan and docile itself; we there only seek to pass away our time... please let it humble itself to us for the nonce."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When scholarly topics enter casual conversation, present learning as supportive and modest rather than authoritative. Anti-pattern: lecturing or preaching in convivial company; prefer adaptable, gentle contributions.
